content_voiceover: Three more practice questions spanning thrombophilia topics. Question fifteen asks which statement about hereditary thrombophilia is wrong, and the flagged answer is C, because the description of factor five Leiden has the amino acid change backwards, the actual mutation replaces arginine five oh six with glutamine, not the reverse phrasing implied, and that arginine five oh six site is the first cleavage site that activated protein C normally uses to inactivate factor five a, which is exactly why the Leiden mutation causes activated protein C resistance. Question forty three, in Chinese, asks which statement about protein C deficient patients is wrong, and the answer is A, because although purified protein C concentrate is not universally available, it is in fact clinically proven and used, particularly for neonatal purpura fulminans and acute thrombotic events in severe protein C deficiency, so saying there is no proven clinically effective concentrate is the false statement. Question forty eight asks which statement about cancer associated thrombosis is wrong, and the answer is A, because hematologic malignancies are actually considered a high risk tumor type for CAT, not a low risk one, this ties directly back to the Hokusai and SELECT-D data you just reviewed, confirming that DOACs show lower recurrent VTE but a trend toward higher bleeding compared to LMWH.
keypoints: Factor V Leiden: Arg506Gln mutation destroys the APC cleavage site on factor Va
This is the mechanistic basis of activated protein C resistance
Purified protein C concentrate IS clinically effective, especially in purpura fulminans
Hematologic malignancies ARE high-risk tumor types for cancer-associated thrombosis
CAT meta-analysis: DOACs lower recurrent VTE, trend toward more bleeding vs LMWH
keypoint_voiceover: Remember factor five Leiden is an arginine five oh six to glutamine substitution that destroys the activated protein C cleavage site, causing APC resistance. Purified protein C concentrate is proven useful in purpura fulminans. And hematologic malignancies are high risk, not low risk, for cancer associated thrombosis.
